name: Traumatic meniscal tear
populations: people with an acute ACL injury
manual workers who squat and twist
summary: An acute tear of the medial or lateral meniscus from twisting on a flexed, weight-bearing knee, causing joint-line pain, delayed swelling and sometimes catching or locking.

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Weight-bearing knee flexion with rotation on a planted foot

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI when surgery is being considered or the knee locks

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Mean ~2 months after partial meniscectomy; ~6 months after repair

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Exercise-first care: clinically relevant improvement by 12 weeks to 12 months

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Adolescents and adults under 40 in pivoting sport

overview:
The menisci are two C-shaped wedges of fibrocartilage that spread load across the tibiofemoral joint, deepen the articulation and contribute to stability. A traumatic meniscal tear is a tear with an acute onset of symptoms caused by a sufficient injury, as opposed to the slowly developing degenerative lesions of middle age [r1]. Most occur when an athlete twists on a flexed, weight-bearing knee; about half are accompanied by other intra-articular injury, most often an ACL rupture [r2].

The outer 10–25% of each meniscus has a blood supply and can heal; the inner portion is avascular and does not [r3]. Losing meniscal tissue raises contact stress on the articular cartilage, which is why preservation (repair, or leaving a stable tear alone) is the first-line goal when surgery is needed [r1]. In young adults, a randomised trial found that early surgery was not superior to 12 weeks of supervised exercise and education with the option of later surgery [r4]. The physiotherapist therefore leads either the first-line exercise program or the criteria-based rehabilitation after repair or meniscectomy.

epidemiology.text: In US high-school athletes, meniscal injuries occurred at 5.1 per 100,000 athlete-exposures, about four times more often in competition than in practice (11.9 vs 2.7). In sports played by both sexes, girls had about twice the rate of boys (5.5 vs 2.5). Contact was the most common mechanism (55.9%), and 54% of injured athletes had other intra-articular pathology [r2]. A meta-analysis found strong evidence that playing soccer or rugby increases the risk of an acute meniscal tear, and that delaying ACL reconstruction for more than 12 months increases the risk of a medial (but not lateral) meniscal tear [r5]. Recurrent giving way in an ACL-deficient knee is the main modifiable risk factor for later medial tears.

intrinsic: ACL deficiency, especially with recurrent giving way; >12 months from ACL injury to reconstruction increases medial meniscal tear risk (modifiable) [r5]
Previous meniscal injury or surgery on the same knee
Discoid lateral meniscus (congenital variant) in children and adolescents
Female sex in sports played by both sexes (higher injury rate) [r2]
Reduced quadriceps strength and neuromuscular control (modifiable)
extrinsic: Pivoting, cutting and contact sports, particularly soccer and rugby [r5]
High shoe–surface traction that fixes the foot while the body rotates
Occupations that combine squatting with twisting

mechanism.summary: The classic non-contact mechanism is rotation of the femur on a fixed tibia while the knee is flexed and loaded, for example twisting to change direction with the foot planted. Axial compression traps the meniscus between the femoral condyle and tibial plateau while rotation and anteroposterior translation shear it. The posterior horn of the medial meniscus is least mobile and is the usual site; the lateral meniscus is more often torn at the time of an acute ACL rupture.
sequence: The foot is planted and fixed by studs or traction while the athlete is weight-bearing on a flexed knee.
The femur rotates on the fixed tibia as the trunk turns (often internal femoral rotation with the knee in 30–90° flexion).
In flexion the femoral condyles roll back, so compressive load concentrates on the posterior horns.
The tethered medial posterior horn cannot escape, and compression plus rotational shear exceed its strength.
A vertical longitudinal tear develops in the posterior horn; with further loading it may extend and the inner fragment can displace into the notch (bucket-handle).
The athlete feels sharp joint-line pain, sometimes a pop or tearing sensation, and often continues playing.
An effusion develops gradually over hours to a day; a displaced fragment may block extension (locked knee).

variants.name: With ACL rupture
variants.description: The pivot-shift subluxation tears the lateral meniscus (often posterior horn) or produces a medial ramp lesion at the meniscocapsular junction. Missed ramp lesions are a cause of persistent instability after ACL reconstruction.

variants.name: Contact (valgus or rotational blow)
variants.description: A tackle or fall onto a flexed, loaded knee combines with an MCL sprain; the medial meniscus is commonly involved.

variants.name: Deep flexion load
variants.description: Rising from a deep squat or kneeling with rotation, typical in manual work and wrestling, loads the posterior horns maximally.

variants.name: Root tear
variants.description: Avulsion of the posterior root from its tibial attachment abolishes hoop function; acute root tears occur with ligament injury, while posterior medial root tears in older adults are often low-energy.

anatomy.text: Each meniscus is a semilunar, wedge-shaped fibrocartilage attached to the tibia at its anterior and posterior roots. Circumferential type I collagen bundles, tied together by radial fibres, convert axial load into hoop stress so that the menisci share load and protect the articular cartilage [r6]. The medial meniscus is C-shaped and less mobile because it is attached to the capsule and deep MCL; the lateral meniscus is more circular and mobile. Branches of the medial, lateral and middle genicular arteries form a perimeniscal plexus that supplies only the peripheral 10–25% of the meniscus. The posterolateral segment beside the popliteus tendon has no penetrating peripheral vessels [r3]. The horns are innervated, so the menisci contribute to pain and proprioception.

structures.name: Medial meniscus
structures.role: Load sharing in the medial compartment; secondary restraint to anterior tibial translation, especially its posterior horn

structures.name: Lateral meniscus
structures.role: Carries a larger share of lateral compartment load; mobile, which helps it escape some injuries

structures.name: Meniscal roots
structures.role: Anchor the horns to the tibia so circumferential fibres can generate hoop stress

structures.name: Perimeniscal capillary plexus
structures.role: Supplies the outer 'red' zone, the only part capable of healing [r3]

structures.name: Articular cartilage
structures.role: Bears the increased contact stress when meniscal function is lost

structures.name: Quadriceps
structures.role: Dynamic shock absorber and key target of rehabilitation; inhibited by effusion

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
The meniscus fails when compressive and shear loads exceed the capacity of its collagen network. Tears that run parallel to the circumferential fibres (vertical longitudinal, bucket-handle) separate bundles without cutting them, so some hoop function survives. Radial and root tears cut across the circumferential fibres and abolish hoop stress, functionally equivalent to removing that segment [r6]. Horizontal and complex patterns are more typical of degenerative tissue.

Healing depends on location. Tears in the vascular outer zone (red–red, and to a lesser extent red–white) can heal with a fibrovascular scar from the perimeniscal plexus, which is why peripheral longitudinal tears are the classic indication for repair. Tears in the inner avascular zone (white–white) have no healing response [r3]. Meniscal deficiency increases peak contact pressures, and meniscal injury is associated with about a four-fold increase in long-term risk of knee osteoarthritis [r5], with about half of patients having radiographic osteoarthritis 10–20 years after injury [r7].

structures.name: Medial meniscus posterior horn
structures.effect: Most common site of a traumatic vertical longitudinal or bucket-handle tear

structures.name: Lateral meniscus
structures.effect: Torn more often at the time of an acute ACL rupture; stable lateral tears left in situ have a relatively good prognosis [r1]

structures.name: Meniscocapsular junction (ramp)
structures.effect: Ramp lesions of the medial posterior horn accompany ACL injury and are easily missed on MRI

structures.name: ACL and MCL
structures.effect: Concomitant ligament injury is common; about half of meniscal injuries in young athletes have associated intra-articular pathology [r2]

structures.name: Articular cartilage
structures.effect: Chondral damage at injury and later overload from lost meniscal function contribute to post-traumatic osteoarthritis [r7]

structures.name: Synovium
structures.effect: Reactive synovitis and effusion from blood and debris in the joint

muscles.name: Quadriceps
muscles.effect: Arthrogenic muscle inhibition from effusion and pain reduces voluntary activation, producing lag, atrophy and persistent weakness [r8]

muscles.name: Hamstrings
muscles.effect: Guarding and protective co-contraction limit terminal extension; may contribute to a flexed-knee gait

muscles.name: Hip abductors and calf
muscles.effect: Disuse weakness from altered gait and reduced activity

cellular.description: Torn peripheral capillaries bleed; a fibrin clot forms in red-zone tears and releases chemotactic and mitogenic factors. Inner-zone tears form no clot attached to vessels [r3].
Vessels from the perimeniscal plexus and undifferentiated mesenchymal cells invade the red-zone clot and lay down fibrovascular scar [r3].
Scar slowly remodels toward fibrocartilage-like tissue; mechanical properties remain below native meniscus for many months.
Avascular inner-zone tears show no healing response; the free edge may fray, propagate or flip, producing catching.

systems.effect: Effusion and altered joint afferent discharge drive spinal reflex inhibition of the quadriceps (AMI) [r8]. Pain arises from the innervated horns, capsule and synovium rather than the avascular inner meniscus.
Synovitis and effusion follow the tear; MRI effusion-synovitis may identify young patients who gain more from early surgery, although this subgroup finding is exploratory [r9].
Patients avoid terminal extension and deep flexion, shift load to the other limb and reduce knee flexion during loading response.
Catching and giving way erode confidence; beliefs that a torn meniscus 'must be removed' influence treatment choice and should be addressed with education.
Meniscal injury and meniscectomy are major drivers of early knee osteoarthritis ('the young patient with an old knee') [r7].

grading.system: Tear pattern and vascular zone (arthroscopic/MRI description)

grades.description: Tear parallel to the circumferential fibres in the peripheral third, typically traumatic.
grades.prognosis: Best healing potential; classic indication for repair [r1]

grades.description: Long longitudinal tear whose inner fragment displaces into the intercondylar notch.
grades.prognosis: Often causes locking; early repair is preferred when possible [r1]

grades.description: Tear from the free edge toward the periphery, cutting circumferential fibres.
grades.prognosis: Loss of hoop function if complete; repair indicated in selected cases

grades.description: Avulsion or radial tear within 1 cm of the root attachment.
grades.prognosis: Functionally equivalent to total meniscectomy; repair gives better outcomes and less osteoarthritis than partial meniscectomy [r10]

grades.description: Tear of the medial meniscocapsular junction of the posterior horn, associated with ACL rupture.
Inner-zone or multiplanar tears; more common in degenerative tissue.
grades.prognosis: Limited healing; managed with exercise or, if mechanically symptomatic, minimal resection

timeframes.summary: Timeframes depend on the pathway. Exercise-first care is reviewed at about 12 weeks; partial meniscectomy allows the fastest return; repair needs months of protected healing. Time is necessary but not sufficient: progression is criteria-based.

healing.description: Effusion, pain and quadriceps inhibition are greatest; fibrin clot forms in peripheral tears
Vascular scar bridges peripheral tears or repairs; loaded deep flexion and pivoting are restricted after repair
Scar matures; strength, power and sport-specific loading are progressed

milestones.label: Full weight-bearing after repair
milestones.note: Most protocols reach full weight-bearing between weeks 4 and 6 [r11]

milestones.label: Return to sport after partial meniscectomy (mean)
Exercise-first review point
milestones.note: 12-week supervised program, then consider surgery if symptoms persist [r4]

milestones.label: Return to sport after repair (mean)
milestones.note: Pooled mean 5.8 months; 6 months is the most common time gate [r11,r12]

timeframes.returnToSport: About 2 months after partial meniscectomy and about 6 months after repair on average, with most athletes returning [r12]. Return is criteria-based, and after repair the surgeon's protocol sets the earliest time.

symptoms: Twisting injury with sharp pain localised to the medial or lateral joint line
Swelling that develops gradually over hours to a day (rather than within 2 hours, which suggests haemarthrosis)
Catching, clicking or a sensation of something moving in the knee
True locking (cannot fully straighten) with a displaced fragment
Pain with deep squatting, kneeling, pivoting and stairs
Giving way, particularly if the ACL is also injured
signs: Joint-line tenderness at the site of the tear
Mild–moderate effusion on stroke or sweep test
Pain at end-range flexion and sometimes a springy block to extension
Pain or a click with rotational provocation (McMurray, Thessaly)
Antalgic gait with reduced knee extension in stance and quadriceps lag

subjective: Mechanism: twisting on a flexed, weight-bearing knee; contact or non-contact; ability to continue playing
Time course of swelling: delayed (meniscus) versus within 2 hours (haemarthrosis: ACL, osteochondral fracture, patellar dislocation)
Mechanical symptoms: distinguish true locking (cannot extend) from pseudo-locking (pain inhibition) and catching
Instability or giving way (associated ACL injury)
Previous knee injury or surgery; age and sport demands
Patient goals, beliefs about surgery and willingness to try a structured exercise program [r4]
observation: Effusion and loss of quadriceps contour
Antalgic gait with the knee held slightly flexed
Inability to lock the knee straight in stance
palpation: Joint-line tenderness at the posteromedial or posterolateral joint line
Effusion grading with the stroke test
MCL and LCL tenderness to identify combined injury
Palpable or visible meniscal cyst at the lateral joint line (horizontal tear)
rangeOfMotion: Compare extension, including hyperextension, with the other side; a springy block suggests a displaced fragment
Flexion is often limited and painful at end range
Pain with passive end-range flexion plus rotation
strength: Quadriceps lag and voluntary activation (straight-leg raise)
Quadriceps and hamstring limb symmetry index (LSI) once the knee is calm
functional: Duck walk and deep squat only late (provocative)
Hop tests once criteria are met

specialTests.name: Joint-line tenderness
specialTests.procedure: With the knee flexed to about 90°, palpate along the medial and lateral joint lines from anterior to posterior and compare with the other knee.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of the patient's pain at the joint line.

specialTests.name: McMurray test
specialTests.purpose: Provoke a click or pain from a torn posterior horn
specialTests.procedure: Patient supine. Fully flex the knee, rotate the tibia externally (medial meniscus) or internally (lateral meniscus) and extend the knee with a valgus or varus stress while palpating the joint line.
specialTests.positive: A painful click or clunk felt at the joint line.

specialTests.name: Thessaly test (20°)
specialTests.procedure: The patient stands on the affected leg with the knee flexed 20°, holding the examiner's hands, and rotates the body and knee internally and externally three times. Test the other leg first.
specialTests.positive: Joint-line pain or a sense of locking or catching.

specialTests.name: Apley compression (grind) test
specialTests.purpose: Compression plus rotation of the menisci
specialTests.procedure: Patient prone with the knee at 90°. Compress the tibia into the femur and rotate it internally and externally; compare with distraction plus rotation.
specialTests.positive: Pain with compression that eases with distraction.

clinicalRules.name: Ottawa knee rules
clinicalRules.description: Use to decide on radiographs in acute knee trauma (age ≥55, isolated patellar or fibular head tenderness, inability to flex to 90°, or inability to weight-bear 4 steps).

outcomeMeasures.name: KOOS (Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score)
outcomeMeasures.use: Pain, symptoms, sport/recreation and quality of life; primary outcome (KOOS4) in the DREAM trial [r4]

outcomeMeasures.name: IKDC Subjective Knee Form
outcomeMeasures.use: Knee function across the rehabilitation course

imaging.indication: Positive Ottawa knee rules, suspected fracture, locked knee or older patient
imaging.findings: Excludes tibial plateau fracture, osteochondral fragment and osteoarthritis; normal in isolated meniscal tears

imaging.indication: When surgery is being considered, the knee is locked, or concomitant injury is suspected; the decision should be made by a musculoskeletal specialist [r1]
imaging.findings: Tear pattern, location (zone), displacement (double-PCL sign in bucket-handle tears), root and ramp lesions, ACL and chondral injury

differentials.name: ACL rupture
differentials.distinguishing: Pop with immediate haemarthrosis within hours and giving way; positive Lachman. Often coexists with a meniscal tear.

differentials.name: MCL sprain
differentials.distinguishing: Valgus mechanism; tenderness along the ligament above or below the joint line; valgus laxity or pain at 30°.

differentials.name: Degenerative meniscal tear
differentials.distinguishing: Over 35 years, no or trivial trauma, gradual onset, often with early osteoarthritis.

differentials.name: Articular cartilage defect
differentials.distinguishing: Activity-related pain and effusion, catching from loose fragments; diagnosed on MRI.

differentials.name: Osteochondritis dissecans
differentials.distinguishing: Skeletally immature or young adult with insidious activity-related pain; lesion on the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle on imaging.

differentials.name: Lateral patellar dislocation
differentials.distinguishing: Twisting injury with rapid haemarthrosis, medial patellar tenderness and a positive apprehension test.

redFlags: Locked knee (a springy block to extension that cannot be overcome): suspect a displaced bucket-handle tear. Arrange urgent orthopaedic review, as early repair gives the best chance of saving the meniscus [r1].
Tense haemarthrosis within 2 hours, giving way or a positive Lachman: assess for ACL rupture, osteochondral fracture or patellar dislocation and refer for MRI and orthopaedic review.
Positive Ottawa knee rules or inability to weight-bear: arrange radiographs to exclude tibial plateau or osteochondral fracture.
Hot, red, swollen knee with fever or no clear injury: suspect septic arthritis or crystal arthropathy. Refer for same-day medical assessment and aspiration.
After surgery, calf pain and swelling (DVT), or wound redness, fever and increasing pain (infection): arrange urgent medical review.

management.principles: Management is guided by symptoms, tear type and the patient's goals rather than by the MRI image alone. Meniscal preservation is the overriding principle: when surgery is needed, repair or leaving a stable tear in situ is preferred to resection because long-term clinical and radiological outcomes are worse after partial meniscectomy [r1]. For young adults without a locked knee, a 12-week supervised exercise and education program with the option of later surgery achieved outcomes similar to early surgery at 12 months; about one in four crossed over to surgery [r4], and this was true for traumatic tears specifically [r14]. A locked knee, a repairable tear with an associated ACL reconstruction, or persistent mechanical symptoms despite good rehabilitation are the main reasons to operate. Discuss the options with the patient using shared decision-making.

medical.name: Meniscal repair
medical.description: Arthroscopic suture repair (inside-out, outside-in or all-inside) of longitudinal, bucket-handle, root, ramp and selected radial tears, ideally performed early. The ESSKA consensus recommends extending repair to many tears previously considered irreparable [r1]. Long-term revision rate is about 19%, and over a third of failures occur after the second year [r15].

medical.name: Root repair (posterior root tears)
medical.description: Transtibial pull-out or anchor repair to restore hoop function. Compared with partial meniscectomy, repair is associated with better Lysholm scores, less severe osteoarthritis and fewer reoperations [r10].

medical.name: Arthroscopic partial meniscectomy
medical.description: Resection of an irreparable, mechanically symptomatic fragment that has failed rehabilitation. It allows faster return to sport but has inferior long-term clinical and radiological outcomes to repair [r1,r12]. It should not be the default for tears that can be repaired.

medical.name: Urgent surgery for a locked knee
medical.description: Arthroscopic reduction and repair (or resection if irreparable) of a displaced bucket-handle fragment that blocks extension.

medical.name: Leaving a stable tear in situ
medical.description: Short, stable tears, particularly lateral tears found at ACL reconstruction, can be left alone; stable lateral tears have a better prognosis than medial tears [r1].

medical.name: Biological augmentation (PRP, needling) of repairs
medical.description: No evidence that platelet-rich plasma or needling improves meniscal healing [r1].

medical.name: Analgesia and short-term NSAIDs
medical.description: Simple analgesia and short NSAID courses to settle pain and effusion and allow quadriceps activation [r8].

physio.name: Supervised exercise therapy and education (first line)
physio.description: 12 weeks of progressive, supervised neuromuscular and strength training (2 sessions/week, plus home exercise) with education about meniscal function and prognosis, and the option of surgery if symptoms persist. Not inferior to early surgery in 18–40-year-olds at 12 months [r4,r14].

physio.name: Criteria-based post-operative rehabilitation
physio.description: Early ROM and progressive weight-bearing after partial meniscectomy; after repair, follow the surgeon's restrictions. In isolated repairs, early ROM and immediate weight-bearing have not been shown to harm healing [r16]. Most protocols start ROM in week 1, reach full ROM by about 6 weeks and full weight-bearing by weeks 4–6 [r11].

physio.name: Quadriceps strengthening and management of AMI
physio.description: Progressive quadriceps loading supported by effusion control, cryotherapy, TENS or NMES to reduce arthrogenic muscle inhibition [r8,r17].

physio.name: Neuromuscular and sport-specific training
physio.description: Balance, landing, cutting and agility progressions before return to sport; address ACL deficiency where present [r17].

physio.name: Education and activity modification
physio.description: Explain that mechanical-sounding symptoms often settle, that MRI findings do not dictate surgery, and that temporary avoidance of deep loaded flexion and pivoting reduces irritation.

physio.name: Prolonged rest or immobilisation
physio.description: Immobilisation and avoiding all loading deepen quadriceps atrophy and stiffness without helping the tear heal.

education: A torn meniscus does not automatically need surgery. Many people do as well with a structured exercise program, with surgery kept as an option.
The outer part of the meniscus has a blood supply and can heal; the inner part cannot, which is why tear location matters.
If your knee locks and you cannot straighten it, seek review promptly.
If surgery is needed, saving the meniscus (repair) is better for the long-term health of the knee than removing it, even though recovery is slower.
Keeping the thigh muscles strong and staying active are the best things you can do to protect the knee long term.

rehab.overview: The same criteria-based stages apply to exercise-first care, rehabilitation after partial meniscectomy and rehabilitation after repair; only the timeframes and precautions differ. Timeframes below are typical for exercise-first care or partial meniscectomy, with repair timeframes in brackets. After repair, the surgeon's protocol (tear type, size and repair technique) always overrides these defaults, and root, radial and complex repairs are usually more restrictive. Use effusion, pain (≤3/10 during, settling within 24 h) and movement quality to guide progression [r17].

stages.name: Settle the knee & restore extension
goals: Full passive extension equal to the other side
Normal gait (after repair, within weight-bearing limits)
precautions: After repair: follow weight-bearing and brace instructions; most protocols allow partial weight-bearing in week 1 and full weight-bearing by weeks 4–6 [r11]
After repair: commonly no loaded flexion beyond 90° for about 4–6 weeks, and no squatting or tibial rotation under load
Avoid forcing painful end-range flexion; respect a springy block (displaced fragment)

exercises.name: Quadriceps sets with towel under heel
exercises.cues: Press the back of the knee down and lift the heel slightly

exercises.name: Heel slides
exercises.cues: Slide slowly into comfortable flexion and back to straight

exercises.name: Straight-leg raise
exercises.cues: Lock the knee straight first, then lift

exercises.name: Stationary bike, high seat
exercises.dosage: 10–15 min, light resistance, once ROM allows

progressionCriteria: Effusion trace or less on stroke test

stages.name: Strength & neuromuscular control
goals: Restore quadriceps, hamstring and hip strength
precautions: After repair: limit loaded squats to about 90° until about 12 weeks unless the surgeon advises otherwise
Progress load only if effusion does not increase the next day

exercises.name: Squat to box (progress depth and load)
exercises.cues: Weight through the whole foot, knee in line with the second toe

exercises.name: Seated knee extension
exercises.cues: Full extension with a 1 s hold at the top

exercises.name: Forward step-up
exercises.cues: Keep the pelvis level and drive through the heel

exercises.name: Glute bridge progressing to single-leg bridge

progressionCriteria: Single-leg squat to 60° with good alignment and no pain
Full ROM (repair: full flexion permitted by surgeon)

stages.name: Running, power & change of direction
goals: Tolerate deep flexion and controlled pivoting
precautions: Introduce deep squats, kneeling and pivoting gradually; these load the posterior horns

exercises.name: Split squat progressing to rear-foot-elevated split squat
Single-leg squat
exercises.cues: Hip back, knee over the foot

exercises.name: Jump squat and drop-landing drills
exercises.cues: Land quietly with hips and knees bent

stages.name: Return to sport
precautions: After repair: do not return to pivoting sport before the surgeon's minimum time (commonly 6 months) [r11]
Monitor workload as training volume rises

exercises.name: Planned then unplanned cutting drills
exercises.cues: Lower the centre of mass; knee over foot

exercises.name: Deceleration and pivot drills
exercises.cues: Turn the hips and foot together

progressionCriteria: Patient-reported function near normal (KOOS sport/recreation) and confidence to return

criteria: No effusion and full, pain-free range of motion
Hop test battery LSI ≥90% with good landing mechanics
Completion of full, unrestricted training including cutting
After repair: surgeon clearance and minimum time elapsed (most commonly 6 months) [r11]
tests: Isokinetic or hand-held dynamometry quadriceps/hamstring LSI
Single, triple, crossover and 6 m timed hop tests
Deep squat and duck walk without pain

prognosis: With exercise-first care, young adults improve by a clinically relevant amount over 12 months, and about one in four go on to surgery [r4]. After surgery, most athletes return to sport: pooled return rates are about 98% after partial meniscectomy and 97% after repair, with 84% and 81% respectively returning to their pre-injury level [r12]. Repairs have a long-term revision rate of about 19% at a mean of 7 years, and 36% of failures occur after the second year [r15]. About half of people with a meniscal tear have radiographic osteoarthritis 10–20 years later [r7], and the risk is greater after meniscectomy than after repair, especially for root tears [r1,r10].
prevention: Neuromuscular warm-up programs that train landing, cutting and balance are used to reduce knee injuries in pivoting sports; evidence for meniscal tears specifically is indirect.
Avoid a long delay before ACL reconstruction in people with recurrent giving way, which increases medial meniscal tear risk [r5].
Maintain quadriceps and hip strength after any knee injury.
clinicalPearls: Swelling within 2 hours suggests haemarthrosis (ACL, osteochondral fracture, patellar dislocation); swelling over the next day is typical of an isolated meniscal tear.
No single test is accurate enough on its own. Combine history (twist, delayed swelling, catching) with joint-line tenderness and Thessaly or McMurray [r13].
Separate true locking (a springy, mechanical block to extension) from pain-inhibited 'pseudo-locking'. Only the first is urgent.
The scan does not decide surgery. Young adults with a non-locked knee can start a 12-week exercise program, with surgery kept for those who do not improve [r4].
After repair, ask the surgeon about tear type and repair technique; root and radial repairs usually need stricter weight-bearing and flexion limits.
Quadriceps weakness outlasts pain. Measure it objectively before running and before return to sport [r8].

animation.title: How a traumatic meniscal tear happens

forces.label: Body weight on a flexed knee
Femur rotates on the fixed tibia

captions.text: A soccer player runs and plants the right foot to change direction.
Studs fix the foot while the knee is bent and carrying body weight.
The body turns, so the femur rotates on the fixed tibia under load.
The meniscus is trapped and sheared between femur and tibia, and it tears.
Sharp joint-line pain; many players carry on, and the knee swells over the next day.
Zooming into the right knee from the front, with the patella reflected.

actions.text: Medial meniscus: tethered to capsule and deep MCL
Displaced bucket-handle can lock the knee

captions.text: The C-shaped medial meniscus is anchored to the capsule, so it cannot slide out of the way.
In flexion the condyle rolls back and loads the posterior horn while rotation shears it.
A vertical longitudinal tear splits the posterior horn along its collagen fibres.
If the tear extends, the inner fragment can flip into the notch: a bucket-handle tear.
Synovitis and a gradual effusion follow over hours to a day.
Pain is felt at the medial joint line, where the tender spot usually lies.
Circumferential collagen bundles, tied by radial fibres, run around the meniscus.
Under load the bundles tense as hoop stress, spreading force over the cartilage.
Compression and shear split the bundles apart along their length.
In the vascular outer 10–25%, vessels bring a clot and cells that bridge the tear with scar.
The avascular inner zone has no blood supply, so tears there cannot heal.
